To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

women who are mothers and/or grandmothers from marginalised urban locales are subjected to intrusive surveillance that impacts upon their ability to make choices around infant feeding and other aspects of motherhood.
The surveillance of motherhood and the policing of women's bodies and behaviours can be understood as part of a moral maze of acceptable femininity.
the surveillance of mothers and grandmothers is a key feature of the contemporary landscape of motherhood.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which women negotiate and resist the policing of motherhood and the ways in which this policing is experienced differently by mothers and grandmothers.
the impact of surveillance upon women’s experiences of motherhood, and the ways in which women negotiate acceptable mothering in a context of moral regulation.
the ways in which women negotiate the surveillance of their bodies, behaviours and choices in relation to infant feeding.

the surveillance of infant feeding and motherhood more widely is a key feature of the moral regulation of women's lives.

the moral maze that is motherhood is a complex, challenging and challenging space for women.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the surveillance of infant feeding practices, and the policing of motherhood, is an important aspect of understanding the contemporary experience of motherhood and its impact on the mothering body.

the surveillance of mothers is a gendered, classed, racialised and sexualised process, which is deeply problematic for the women we interviewed, who were already marginalised by virtue of their class, gender and ethnicity.
women's experiences of mothering and infant feeding are mediated by the surveillance of their everyday lives.
The main takeaway from our work is that

women are not passive recipients of these messages; instead, they actively negotiate and navigate their way through the maze, often using their own experiences and those of their own mother as a guide.

the policing of infant feeding is a gendered experience that impacts on women's sense of self and belonging in the community, and that this policing is intensified for women who do not fit into the 'right' categories of mothering, such as those with a disability or those from a working-class background.
the policing of women's behaviour, and the surveillance that this engenders, has significant consequences for the everyday lives of mothers.
